Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It infects leaves and fruit, causing olive-green velvety spots that turn dark brown or black.
symptoms: Dull olive-green to brown velvety spots on upper leaf surfaces
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and turn yellow before premature drop
Cork-like scabby lesions on developing fruit

recommendations.cultural: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering fungal ascospores. Prune canopy to improve air circulation and rapid drying.
recommendations.organic: Apply sulfur or copper-based fungicides early in the spring at bud break. Neem oil can reduce spore germination.
recommendations.chemical: Use preventative fungicides containing myclobutanil, captan, or mancozeb according to local agricultural extension spray schedules.
recommendations.prevention: Plant resistant cultivars (such as Honeycrisp, Enterprise, or Liberty) and avoid overhead irrigation.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. On leaves, it produces characteristic 'frogeye' spots with tan centers and purple margins.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves expanding into circular lesions with light brown/tan centers
Severe defoliation weakening tree vigor
Black sunken cankers on twigs and limbs
Firm brown to black rotting fruit with concentric rings

recommendations.cultural: Prune dead wood, remove mummified fruit, and cut out branch cankers at least 15 cm below visible infection.
recommendations.organic: Liquid copper soap sprays during dormancy and early leaf emergence.
recommendations.chemical: Apply captan, thiophanate-methyl, or strobilurin fungicides during petal fall and cover sprays.
recommendations.prevention: Sanitize pruning tools between cuts with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach solution.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A heteroecious fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae requiring both apple and Eastern red cedar/juniper trees to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish spots on the upper leaf surface
Small raised orange-brown tubular projections (aecia) on the underside of leaves
Premature leaf yellowing and shedding in summer

recommendations.cultural: Remove nearby cedar/juniper trees within a 1-2 mile radius if practical, or prune out cedar galls before spring rains.
recommendations.organic: Sulfur sprays applied preventively as flower buds show pink color through petal fall.
recommendations.chemical: Systemic fungicides containing myclobutanil or propiconazole applied at 7-10 day intervals during early spring.
recommendations.prevention: Choose rust-resistant apple varieties such as Freedom, Redfree, or William's Pride.

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays clean, vibrant green coloring with normal leaf turgor and no symptoms of fungal, bacterial, or viral infection.
symptoms: Uniform deep green leaf coloration
Smooth margins with no necrotic lesions or chlorosis
Vigorous shoot growth and healthy leaf canopy

recommendations.cultural: Maintain balanced annual fertilization, regular soil testing, and optimal pruning for sunlight penetration.
recommendations.organic: Apply compost mulch around the drip line to conserve soil moisture and boost beneficial soil microbes.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring for early pest or pathogen detection.
recommendations.prevention: Follow good orchard sanitation and maintain adequate tree spacing.

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant is in peak physiological health with undamaged leaves and characteristic rich green foliage.
symptoms: Consistent dark green or waxy foliage
Absence of spots, leaf curl, or marginal scorch
Healthy active shoot expansion

recommendations.cultural: Ensure acidic soil conditions (pH 4.5 to 5.2) using elemental sulfur or peat moss. Mulch heavily with pine needles or bark.
recommendations.organic: Provide consistent moisture using drip irrigation; blueberries are shallow-rooted.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical intervention needed.
recommendations.prevention: Conduct annual soil pH and fertility tests.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Caused by Podosphaera clandestina. It affects young leaves and green fruit, presenting as patches of white powdery fungal mycelium.
symptoms: White talcum-powder-like patches on lower leaf surfaces and young shoots
Upward curling, distortion, and blistering of expanding leaves
Stunted shoot terminal growth and blemished fruit

recommendations.cultural: Prune dense canopies to maximize light interception and airflow. Avoid excessive late-season nitrogen applications.
recommendations.organic: Spray potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or wettable sulfur at the first sign of mildew.
recommendations.chemical: Apply quinoxyfen, myclobutanil, or triflumizole starting at shuck fall if disease pressure is high.
recommendations.prevention: Monitor young water sprouts regularly where mildew initiates.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Cherry foliage is vigorous, unblemished, and free of mildew or spot symptoms.
symptoms: Bright green lustrous leaves
No fungal growth, spots, or leaf perforation (shot-hole)
Strong terminal shoot elongation

recommendations.cultural: Ensure deep periodic watering during dry periods and keep tree base free of competing weeds.
recommendations.organic: Apply organic mulch around base keeping collar clear.
recommendations.chemical: No treatment required.
recommendations.prevention: Prune during dry summer weather to reduce bacterial canker risk.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is one of the most yield-destructive corn foliar diseases under warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Rectangular lesions delimited by leaf veins with distinct sharp borders
Lesions transition from tan to gray as fungal sporulation occurs
Extensive leaf blighting leading to premature lodging and reduced grain fill

recommendations.cultural: Implement crop rotation with non-host crops (soybean, sorghum). Utilize tillage to bury infected crop residue where soil conservation allows.
recommendations.organic: Biological seed treatments and biofungicides (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens).
recommendations.chemical: Apply strobilurin (azoxystrobin) or triazole (propiconazole) fungicides at tassel (VT) to silking (R1) stage.
recommendations.prevention: Select corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance or resistance ratings.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Caused by Puccinia sorghi. Spores are carried long distances by wind currents from southern regions during cool, moist periods.
symptoms: Small circular to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture epidermal tissue, releasing powdery reddish-brown urediniospores
Severe infections cause leaves to yellow and chlorose

recommendations.cultural: Plant early in the season to escape peak spore dispersal periods.
recommendations.organic: Encourage canopy airflow and avoid excessive high-density seeding.
recommendations.chemical: Foliar fungicides containing pyraclostrobin or tebuconazole if rust reaches the ear leaf before blister stage.
recommendations.prevention: Plant resistant hybrids possessing Rp resistance genes.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Caused by Exserohilum turcicum (Setosphaeria turcica). Develops during moderate temperatures accompanied by prolonged wetness.
symptoms: Large cigar-shaped or elliptical grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long)
Dark olive sporulation visible within lesion centers during damp weather
Lesions coalesce, causing extensive foliage death

recommendations.cultural: Rotate away from continuous corn; manage corn residue through vertical tillage or grazing.
recommendations.organic: Copper compounds early in smallholder settings; bio-protective microbial inoculants.
recommendations.chemical: Apply dual-action fungicides (strobilurin + triazole) when lesions appear on or below ear leaf around tasseling.
recommendations.prevention: Utilize corn hybrids carrying Ht gene resistance.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The maize plant exhibits robust development, lush broad green leaves, and no visual foliar blights.
symptoms: Broad, uniformly emerald green leaves with intact leaf margins
No pustules, streaks, or elongated necrotic lesions
Stout stalks with strong brace root formation

recommendations.cultural: Maintain optimal nitrogen side-dressing and weed management.
recommendations.organic: Incorporate green manures or cover crops in crop rotation.
recommendations.chemical: No treatment required.
recommendations.prevention: Scout fields bi-weekly through reproduction stages.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Caused by Guignardia bidwellii. Highly destructive to fruit clusters and can defoliate vines during warm, wet growing seasons.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown circular spots on leaves with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia)
Dark elongated lesions on petioles and shoots
Berries shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies

recommendations.cultural: Destroy all mummified grape clusters during winter pruning. Maintain an open vine canopy to promote rapid drying.
recommendations.organic: Apply copper hydroxide or lime sulfur before bloom and during fruit set.
recommendations.chemical: Apply myclobutanil, kresoxim-methyl, or mancozeb from early shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom.
recommendations.prevention: Remove wild Vitis species within 100 meters of the vineyard.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A complex fungal trunk disease involving Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and Fomitiporia mediterranea.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between green leaf veins
Dark brown to purple spots ('measles') on white or red grape berry skins
Sudden vine apoplexy (complete vine collapse) during hot dry weather

recommendations.cultural: Prune late in the dormant season and avoid pruning during rain. Paint pruning wounds with sealant.
recommendations.organic: Trichoderma-based wound protectors applied immediately following pruning cuts.
recommendations.chemical: No cure exists once established in heartwood; remedial surgery (trunk renewal) can extend vine lifespan.
recommendations.prevention: Purchase certified pathogen-free rootstock and nursery vines.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis clavispora). Occurs late in the season, causing premature vine senescence.
symptoms: Angular, dark brown to black spots with yellowish borders on upper leaf surfaces
Dark velvety fungal growth on lesion undersides
Premature leaf drop leading to delayed wood hardening

recommendations.cultural: Collect and burn fallen leaves after harvest. Ensure good trellis ventilation.
recommendations.organic: Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate and slaked lime) applied post-harvest.
recommendations.chemical: Apply broad-spectrum fungicides such as captan or folpet if defoliation begins before harvest.
recommendations.prevention: Maintain vine canopy height and prune lateral shoots.

Grape___healthy.description: Grapevine canopy is in peak condition with undamaged fan-shaped leaves and well-formed clusters.
symptoms: Uniform deep green, palmate leaves without discoloration
Smooth canes and healthy tendril development
No spotting, fruit mummification, or vein chlorosis

recommendations.cultural: Perform canopy shoot positioning and regular leaf pulling in the fruit zone for sunlight exposure.
recommendations.organic: Apply composted vineyard pomace to enrich topsoil fertility.
recommendations.chemical: No treatment required.
recommendations.prevention: Maintain vineyard floor groundcover to mitigate soil erosion.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A devastating bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri).
symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy yellow mottling across leaf veins
Yellowing of individual shoots ('yellow dragon')
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end
Progressive branch dieback and eventual tree decline

recommendations.cultural: Scout rigorously for Asian citrus psyllids. Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees immediately to protect neighboring groves.
recommendations.organic: Release parasitic wasps (Tamarixia radiata) to biological control psyllid populations.
recommendations.chemical: Target psyllid vectors with systemic neonicotinoids or pyrethroids during flush cycles. Foliar nutritional sprays.
recommendations.prevention: Propagate exclusively inside certified insect-proof screenhouses using tested budwood.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Infects leaves, twigs, and fruit, particularly in sandy soils during wet spring conditions.
symptoms: Small angular water-soaked lesions that turn purple to dark brown
Centres of spots drop out, creating a 'shot-hole' appearance
Gum exudation and pitting on ripening peaches

recommendations.cultural: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces susceptible succulent foliage. Establish windbreaks to mitigate windblown sand injury.
recommendations.organic: Low-rate copper applications during dormancy and bud swell.
recommendations.chemical: Oxytetracycline (Mycoshield) sprays during bloom and petal fall if copper phytotoxicity is a concern.
recommendations.prevention: Plant resistant varieties such as Redhaven, Biscoe, or Candor.

Peach___healthy.description: The peach tree displays healthy lanceolate foliage with clean green surfaces and strong terminal growth.
symptoms: Slender, bright green lance-shaped leaves with uniform texture
No shot-hole punctures, curling, or gummy exudates
Vigorous shoot growth and clean bark

recommendations.cultural: Maintain open center (vase) pruning system to maximize interior canopy light.
recommendations.organic: Apply mulch around tree dripline to conserve water.
recommendations.chemical: No spray required.
recommendations.prevention: Monitor for peach tree borer and spring frost protection.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria. Spreads rapidly through wind-driven rain, splashing water, and handling wet plants.
symptoms: Small circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaves turning brown with greasy margins
Severely affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, exposing fruit to sunscald
Rough blister-like raised brown scabs on bell peppers

recommendations.cultural: Avoid overhead watering; switch to drip irrigation. Do not work in fields when leaves are wet. Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants for 2+ years.
recommendations.organic: Apply fixed copper bactericides combined with bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis.
recommendations.chemical: Tank-mix copper with mancozeb to increase bactericidal efficacy and mitigate resistance.
recommendations.prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed and soak seeds in hot water (50°C for 25 min) before planting.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Bell pepper plant exhibits dark green lush foliage, sturdy stems, and no viral or bacterial spot symptoms.
symptoms: Lustrous dark green leaves with uniform surface
No spotting, curling, blistering, or defoliation
Strong branching and abundant blossom set

recommendations.cultural: Provide consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom end rot (calcium uptake deficiency). Stake plants to support fruit load.
recommendations.organic: Apply organic mulch around plants and compost tea.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical treatment needed.
recommendations.prevention: Maintain soil calcium and regular balanced fertilizing.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Primarily targets older, stressed lower leaves and develops in warm, alternating wet and dry conditions.
symptoms: Dark brown to black concentric circular rings creating a characteristic 'target-board' or 'bullseye' appearance
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding lesions
Lower leaves senesce and die prematurely, reducing tuber bulk

recommendations.cultural: Maintain adequate vine nutrition, especially nitrogen. Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers. Rotate away from potatoes/tomatoes for 3 years.
recommendations.organic: Foliar sprays of copper fungicides or potassium bicarbonate.
recommendations.chemical: Preventative protectants (chlorothalonil or mancozeb) alternated with translaminar fungicides (difenoconazole, azoxystrobin).
recommendations.prevention: Harvest tubers only after vine maturity to prevent spore contact with tuber skins.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans (the pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine). Capable of destroying entire fields in days under cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large dark brown to purplish-black water-soaked lesions expanding rapidly across leaves
Delicate white cottony mildew growth on lesion undersides during high humidity
Foul decomposing odor in severely blighted fields; tubers develop firm dry brown rot

recommendations.cultural: Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles. Avoid field work when foliage is wet. Kill vines 2 weeks before tuber harvest.
recommendations.organic: Strict preventative copper hydroxide applications prior to rainy periods; bio-control Bacillus subtilis.
recommendations.chemical: Apply systemic and translaminar oomycete fungicides: metalaxyl, cymoxanil, mandipropamid, or fluopicolide.
recommendations.prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers and monitor regional late blight forecasting warnings.

Potato___healthy.description: Potato foliage is dense, dark green, and free of concentric lesions or water-soaked blights.
symptoms: Robust compound leaves with uniform green tint
No spotting, chlorosis, or underside mold
Vigorous vine canopy indicating active tuber bulking

recommendations.cultural: Hill up soil around stems to prevent tubers from greening and to block spore migration from soil.
recommendations.organic: Maintain regular weeding and consistent soil moisture.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical application needed.
recommendations.prevention: Sanitize equipment between fields to avoid transmitting soil-borne pathogens.

Raspberry___healthy.description: Raspberry canes and compound leaves are vigorous, unblemished, and in prime physiological state.
symptoms: Vibrant green serrated foliage without rust spots or yellow veins
Erect, healthy primocanes and floricanes
Clean leaf petioles without lesions

recommendations.cultural: Trellis canes to keep foliage off the ground and improve airflow. Prune out spent floricanes after fruiting.
recommendations.organic: Mulch root zone to maintain cool, moist conditions.
recommendations.chemical: No treatment required.
recommendations.prevention: Maintain proper plant spacing (45-60 cm apart).

Soybean___healthy.description: Soybean trifoliate leaves display complete health, strong photosynthetic capacity, and absence of foliar pathogens.
symptoms: Uniform medium-to-dark green trifoliate leaves
Absence of pustules, frogeye spots, or sudden death syndrome chlorosis
Strong nodulation at root crown

recommendations.cultural: Ensure balanced soil potassium and phosphorus. Implement timely weed suppression.
recommendations.organic: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting.
recommendations.chemical: No fungicide needed.
recommendations.prevention: Rotate crops with corn or small grains.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Caused by Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea). Common in cucurbit crops in high humidity or shaded canopy conditions.
symptoms: White powdery fungal spots resembling talcum powder on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Leaves turn yellow, brown, and brittle, leading to premature leaf scorch
Sunscald and poor flavor development on exposed squash fruit

recommendations.cultural: Space plants generously to promote rapid drying. Plant in full sun with drip irrigation.
recommendations.organic: Spray potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or diluted milk solution (1:9 ratio with water) preventatively.
recommendations.chemical: Apply systemic fungicides such as triflumizole, myclobutanil, or boscalid at the first sign of mildew colonies.
recommendations.prevention: Select powdery mildew-resistant (PMR) squash hybrids.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Caused by Diplocarpon earlianum. Affects strawberry foliage, calyxes, and stolons, reducing plant vigor and winter hardiness.
symptoms: Irregular dark purple to reddish-brown spots without white centers
Spots coalesce, causing entire leaf blades to turn purplish-brown and curl up at margins ('scorched' appearance)
Browning of fruit calyx caps

recommendations.cultural: Mow and remove old leaves immediately following renovation of June-bearing beds. Avoid overhead irrigation.
recommendations.organic: Copper-based fungicidal sprays during early spring emergence.
recommendations.chemical: Apply captan or thiophanate-methyl when new leaf growth initiates in spring.
recommendations.prevention: Plant disease-free runner plants and renovate beds annually.

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry plant possesses robust, emerald trifoliate foliage with clean leaf margins and vigorous crown development.
symptoms: Lustrous deep green trifoliate leaflets
No purple blemishes, leaf spot eyes, or edge burning
Clean crown and productive runner development

recommendations.cultural: Keep beds well weeded and straw-mulched to protect fruit from soil splash.
recommendations.organic: Side-dress with balanced organic compost in early spring.
recommendations.chemical: No treatment required.
recommendations.prevention: Replace plantings every 3-4 years to avoid soil pathogen accumulation.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Caused by Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas vesicatoria. Highly infectious and spreads rapidly in warm, rainy, and humid environments.
symptoms: Small (2-3 mm) dark brown to black circular lesions that look greasy or water-soaked
Lesions surrounded by yellow halos; leaves become torn and ragged
Blister-like, raised, scab-like spots on green and ripe tomatoes

recommendations.cultural: Avoid overhead watering; irrigate strictly at the base via drip lines. Do not touch or prune plants when wet. Sanitize stakes and cages.
recommendations.organic: Fixed copper bactericides combined with Bacillus subtilis or bacteriophage sprays.
recommendations.chemical: Copper hydroxide mixed with mancozeb applied at 7-day intervals during warm, wet weather.
recommendations.prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants; practice a 3-year crop rotation.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. A ubiquitous disease starting on older, lower foliage and gradually progressing upward.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings resembling a target board
Pronounced yellow chlorotic halos surrounding lesions
Lower leaves yellow, wither, and drop prematurely, leaving fruit vulnerable to sunscald

recommendations.cultural: Mulch soil around tomato bases with straw or plastic to prevent rain splash. Prune bottom 30 cm of leaves to enhance airflow.
recommendations.organic: Apply copper octanoate, sulfur, or serenade biofungicide at the first appearance of lower spots.
recommendations.chemical: Preventative chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin rotated with difenoconazole.
recommendations.prevention: Clean up and compost or burn all tomato vines at season's end; rotate crops for at least 2-3 years.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. A devastating oomycete that can kill entire tomato plants and gardens within a week under cool, rainy conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked, dark olive to black lesions that enlarge rapidly
White fungal-like fuzzy mold visible on the underside of leaves during damp mornings
Stems turn dark brown or greasy black; fruit develops firm, leathery, dark brown patches

recommendations.cultural: Immediately bag and discard infected plants in municipal waste (do not compost). Space plants widely and ensure maximum sunlight.
recommendations.organic: Preventative copper fungicide applied prior to anticipated rainy periods.
recommendations.chemical: Systemic fungicides such as cymoxanil, dimethomorph, or mandipropamid for commercial or severe outbreaks.
recommendations.prevention: Select late-blight-resistant varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Merit, Jasper) and monitor regional alerts.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Caused by Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva). Predominantly troublesome in greenhouse and high-tunnel environments with relative humidity above 85%.
symptoms: Pale green to pale yellow chlorotic spots on the upper leaf surface with indistinct borders
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth directly underneath on the lower leaf surface
Leaves curl, wither, and drop from bottom to top

recommendations.cultural: Lower humidity in greenhouses below 80% using ventilation, horizontal airflow fans, and morning heating.
recommendations.organic: Copper-based sprays or bio-fungicide Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
recommendations.chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, thiophanate-methyl, or cyazofamid if humidity cannot be controlled.
recommendations.prevention: Plant resistant cultivars possessing Cf resistance genes and prune dense sucker growth.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Caused by Septoria lycopersici. One of the most destructive leaf diseases of tomatoes in wet seasons, causing severe defoliation without directly infecting fruit.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 - 3 mm) circular spots with dark brown margins and sunken grayish-white centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) clearly visible in the centers of spots with a magnifying glass
Severe lower leaf yellowing, drying up, and premature dropping

recommendations.cultural: Avoid overhead irrigation; water only at the soil line. Prune lower branches. Apply organic mulch to stop spore splash from soil.
recommendations.organic: Foliar copper sprays applied at 7-10 day intervals starting at early blossom set.
recommendations.chemical: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb alternated with strobilurins.
recommendations.prevention: Strict 3-year crop rotation and thorough autumn garden cleanup.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Pest infestation by Tetranychus urticae. Rapidly multiplies during hot, dry, and dusty conditions, sucking sap from leaf cells.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) on the upper leaf surface
Fine silken webbing on leaf undersides, growing tips, and stems
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, become papery, and drop prematurely

recommendations.cultural: Hose down leaf undersides with strong water spray to dislodge mites and reduce dust. Keep plants well watered.
recommendations.organic: Apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or horticultural oils. Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
recommendations.chemical: Apply specific miticides (abamectin, bifenazate, or spiromesifen); avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators.
recommendations.prevention: Eliminate broadleaf weeds (e.g., mallow, pigweed) around borders that serve as mite reservoirs.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Affects leaves, stems, and fruit, thriving in warm, humid tropical and subtropical climates.
symptoms: Small pinpoint brown spots on upper leaves enlarging into brown lesions with light brown centers and faint concentric rings
Lesions lack the pronounced chlorotic halos typical of early blight
Sunken crater-like spots on green and ripe fruit

recommendations.cultural: Stake plants and maintain wide row spacing. Remove sucker growth to maximize air circulation.
recommendations.organic: Apply copper fungicides before canopy closure.
recommendations.chemical: Foliar sprays containing fluxapyroxad, pyraclostrobin, or azoxystrobin.
recommendations.prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous and non-leguminous crops.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A devastating begomovirus transmitted by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Infected young plants rarely produce marketable fruit.
symptoms: Pronounced upward curling and cupping of leaflets
Severe marginal and interveinal yellowing (chlorosis)
Severe stunting of shoots, giving plants an erect, bushy 'bonsai' appearance
Heavy flower drop and abortion of fruit set

recommendations.cultural: Eradicate infected plants immediately and seal in plastic bags. Install 50-mesh insect netting in greenhouses.
recommendations.organic: Use yellow sticky cards for whitefly trapping; apply insecticidal soap or neem oil to reduce vectors.
recommendations.chemical: Target whitefly vectors with systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, acetamiprid) at seedling stage.
recommendations.prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tycoon, Camaro, Securitas) and maintain vector-free nursery stock.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A highly stable, mechanically transmitted tobamovirus. Spreads readily on hands, tools, clothing, and through smoker's tobacco residue.
symptoms: Mottling of leaves with alternating light and dark green mosaic patterns
Leaf distortion, blistering, and 'shoestring' fern-like malformation
Stunted plant growth and uneven fruit ripening with internal brown browning

recommendations.cultural: Wash hands with soap and water before handling plants. Prohibit tobacco use near tomatoes. Sanitize pruning tools in 20% nonfat dry milk or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP).
recommendations.organic: Milk sprays (protein binds virus particles); remove and destroy infected plants promptly.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical virucides exist. Management relies entirely on vector control and strict sanitation.
recommendations.prevention: Purchase certified seed tested free of ToMV or treat seed in hot water (70°C for 3 days) or 10% TSP. Select resistant varieties labeled 'ToMV'.

Tomato___healthy.description: Tomato foliage displays optimal physiological health, dark green color, balanced turgor, and zero signs of pathogen infestation.
symptoms: Lush, deeply divided pinnate leaves with vibrant green coloration
Clean leaf surfaces without spots, mosaics, or marginal scorch
Strong vertical stem growth with active flower trusses

recommendations.cultural: Maintain consistent deep watering (2.5-5 cm per week) to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking. Prune lower suckers regularly.
recommendations.organic: Apply organic mulch (straw or compost) around the base to preserve moisture and suppress weeds.
recommendations.chemical: No chemical treatment needed. Continue weekly scouting for hornworms and early blight signs.
recommendations.prevention: Rotate tomato planting locations annually and stake plants securely.
